extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students and practitioners of public relations
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative principles relevant to crafting public-relations messages (including press releases): audience targeting, messaging consistency, ethical transparency, channel and timing choices, and avoidance of deceptive spin or astroturfing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy and openness (Ivy Lee Declaration of Principles)
rubrics_metrics.description: Public relations work should be done in the open, should be accurate and cover topics of public interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ivy Lee is credited with developing the modern press release and the 'two-way-street' philosophy of both listening to and communicating with respective publics. Press releases and other PR outputs should therefore aim for accuracy, openness, and public-interest relevance rather than secrecy or deliberate misinformation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience targeting
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify the target audience, and tailor messages to appeal to each audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sometimes differing audiences/common stakeholders necessitate creation of several distinct but complementary messages. Practitioners should distinguish between stakeholders (those with a stake in an institution or issue) and audiences (those likely to receive or act on a particular message) when designing releases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Messaging consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: Messaging is the process of creating a consistent story around a product, person, company or service.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Messaging aims to avoid having readers receive contradictory or confusing information that will instill doubt. Brands aim to have the same problem statement, industry viewpoint or brand perception shared across sources and mediums — press releases should support that consistent story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-way communication model choice (asymmetrical vs symmetrical)
rubrics_metrics.description: Two-way communications in social media (and PR) can be asymmetrical or symmetrical: asymmetrical uses public feedback to persuade the public to change; symmetrical seeks a balance between the organization's interests and the public's interests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether a press release or campaign will primarily attempt to persuade (asymmetrical) or to engage and accommodate public interests (symmetrical). The model chosen affects tone, content, and willingness to incorporate public concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical codes and professional conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: The field is generally highly un-regulated, but many professionals voluntarily adhere to codes of conduct published by professional bodies (e.g., PRSA, Chartered Institute of Public Relations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adherence to ethical codes affects credibility: the public often distrusts paid communicators (Edelman survey cited). Press releases should therefore follow professional ethical standards to avoid misleading the public and to preserve reputation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of spin and deceptive techniques
rubrics_metrics.description: Spin refers to providing a certain interpretation meant to sway public opinion; techniques include cherry picking facts, the 'non-denial denial', euphemisms, ambiguity, and selective timing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spin is a derogatory term in the profession (implying deceit). Press releases should avoid these techniques if ethical transparency and credibility are priorities. Be aware that timing and selective presentation can be used manipulatively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency about front groups and astroturfing
rubrics_metrics.description: When a lobby group hides its true purpose and support base it is known as a front group; front groups are a form of astroturfing intended to sway the public or government without disclosing financial connections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Press releases and campaigns should disclose sponsorship and avoid disguising sponsored messages as independent grassroots opinion; failing to disclose creates ethical and reputational risks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of channels and multimedia (press releases among tactics)
rubrics_metrics.description: Typical public relations activities include press releases, newsletters, blogs, social media, press kits, and the production/distribution of video and audio news releases (VNRs and ANRs) to TV outlets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select channels based on audience and media trends (decline of traditional print, rise of social and online media). Use appropriate formats (text, press kits, VNRs) to increase pickup by target outlets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing and release strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: Careful choice of timing in the release of certain news can take advantage of prominent events in the news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Timing is both a tactical consideration for maximizing coverage and a technique sometimes used manipulatively (to distract or minimize scrutiny). Plan release timing to align with news cycles and audience attention while avoiding deceptive timing tactics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crisis communication responsiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: Crisis communication — responding in a crisis — is a specific PR discipline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Social media has increased the speed of breaking news and created greater time constraints on responses. Press releases used in crises should be fast, accurate, coordinated with wider crisis strategy, and mindful of real-time social channels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Building and managing influencer/media relationships
rubrics_metrics.description: Building and managing relationships with those who influence an organization or individual's audiences has a central role in doing public relations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experienced practitioners accumulate lists of media and influencer relationships that become an asset. Press release distribution and pitching should leverage those relationships to increase likelihood of pickup.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define objectives and implement planned programs of action
rubrics_metrics.description: Public relations defined as 'a management function, which tabulates public attitudes, defines the policies, procedures, and interests of an organization... followed by executing a program of action to earn public understanding and acceptance.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Press releases should be part of a planned program with measurable objectives aimed at earning understanding and acceptance; align releases with organizational policies and strategic goals and consider public interest outcomes (per World Assembly definition).

rubrics_metrics.name: Propaganda characteristics to avoid (one-sided, selective, emotional appeals)
rubrics_metrics.description: Propaganda presents only one side of an argument, often selectively presenting facts or using loaded messages to produce an emotional rather than rational response, repeated across media to change audience attitudes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While some propaganda can be benign (public health messages), press releases should avoid one-sided, manipulative messaging if ethical communication and credibility are desired. Recognize the distinction between informative persuasion and manipulative propaganda.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of social-science insights (ethical considerations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Bernays viewed public relations as an 'applied social science' using psychology, sociology and other disciplines to manage and manipulate the thinking and behavior of the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applying social-science insights can improve effectiveness (e.g., framing, appeals), but practitioners should weigh ethical implications — examples like 'Torches of Freedom' illustrate how psychological tactics can be used without the audience's informed consent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stakeholder vs audience distinction for targeting
rubrics_metrics.description: All audiences are stakeholders (or presumptive stakeholders), but not all stakeholders are audiences; e.g., a charity's stakeholders include those with the disease, but the audience for a fundraising release is donors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the distinction to clarify who a particular release is trying to reach and what action or response is expected from that audience; tailor content, calls-to-action, and channels accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Professionalization, standards and training
rubrics_metrics.description: The profession developed textbooks, vocational courses, trade associations (PRSA, Chartered Institute) and ethical codes — indicating professional norms and standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Press release authors should be familiar with professional standards and training resources; institutionalizing standards (style, accuracy, disclosure) helps maintain credibility and consistent practice across practitioners.
